definition: A job interview, usually 45 to 60 minutes, in which a candidate designs a large software system out loud: clarifying requirements, estimating load, sketching components and discussing trade-offs. It tests reasoning and communication more than knowledge of one "right" answer.
example: In a URL-shortener interview you are expected to size the traffic, design the API and dive deep into how unique short codes are generated.

definition: The daily rise and fall of traffic as users in a region wake, work and sleep. It is one reason peak load is several times the daily average.
example: A UK-only service may see little traffic at 4 am and its peak in the early evening.

definition: The digits of a number that carry meaning about its precision. Estimates usually need only one or two.
example: 86,400 to one significant figure is 90,000.

definition: In replicated data, whether every reader sees the latest successful write. Strong consistency means reads always reflect the latest write; weaker models allow briefly stale reads in exchange for speed and availability.
example: After a strongly consistent write, a read from any replica returns the new value.

definition: Describes a system in which replicas may briefly disagree after a write but converge on the same value once updates stop arriving. See eventual consistency.
example: Two users seeing slightly different suggestion lists for a few minutes is acceptable in an eventually consistent typeahead.

definition: The HTTP status code meaning a resource is permanently gone. APNs returns it when a device token is no longer active for the topic.
example: A push sender seeing 410 for a token should stop sending to that registration.

definition: Asking a server repeatedly at fixed intervals whether anything has changed. Short intervals waste requests; long ones add delay.
example: 250 million clients polling every 2 seconds would send 125 million requests a second.

definition: The way an application reads and writes data: which lookups it does, by what key, how often and in what order. Access patterns, not fashion, should decide the data store and partition key.
example: "Get the last 50 messages in a conversation" is a range scan within one partition.

definition: In wide-column stores such as Cassandra, the column that orders rows inside a partition, so range scans in that order are fast. DynamoDB calls it the sort key.
example: Clustering by seq keeps a conversation's messages in sequence order.

definition: Reading a single record by its exact key, as opposed to scanning a range.
example: code → long URL is a point lookup.

definition: Reading every record whose key falls between two values, in key order, for example all messages in one conversation older than a given sequence number.
example: Fetching messages 900 to 950 of a conversation is a range scan.

definition: An extra index that lets you look records up by a field other than the main key. In DynamoDB a GSI has its own partition key and is updated asynchronously.
example: A GSI on owner_id answers "list my links".

definition: Uneven distribution of data, traffic or activity: a few keys, partitions, servers or accounts carry most of it, so averages mislead and the busiest part sets the limits.
example: Far more English queries start with "s" than with "x", so sharding by first letter is skewed.

definition: Disk space the operating system uses to hold memory pages when RAM runs out. Reading a swapped-out page is roughly a thousand times slower than RAM or worse, which ruins tail latency.
example: A trie bigger than the machine's RAM, with swap enabled, turns sub-microsecond memory reads into disk reads of a hundred microseconds or more.

definition: Extra memory a program or data store uses beyond the raw data: pointers, object headers, hash tables and allocator padding. It can multiply the raw estimate several times.
example: A 16-byte timeline entry may take far more than 16 bytes inside Redis.

definition: The full set of names or identifiers that could be issued. Occupancy is the fraction already in use, which sets collision and guessing odds.
example: At 10% namespace occupancy, one random code in ten is already taken.

definition: A 64-bit ID scheme from Twitter: a millisecond timestamp, a machine ID and a per-millisecond sequence number. Machines generate unique, roughly time-ordered IDs without coordinating.
example: Snowflake gives each worker 4,096 IDs per millisecond.

definition: Handing each server a block of IDs (say a million) from a central counter, which it then issues from memory. The coordinator is contacted once per block instead of once per ID.
example: At 3,000 writes a second a million-ID block lasts about five and a half minutes.

definition: A small, highly available service that holds shared configuration, locks, leader election or counters for a fleet, typically ZooKeeper or etcd.
example: The ID coordinator hands out non-overlapping ID blocks to write servers.

definition: Two different inputs producing the same output from a hash or code generator. In a finite code space collisions are inevitable once enough items exist and must be detected.
example: Two URLs whose truncated hashes are both "Qx81bKa" collide.

definition: The probability result that repeats appear surprisingly early when drawing at random: in a space of N values, a 50% chance of a repeat arrives after only about 1.18 × √N draws.
example: Just 23 people give a 50% chance that two share a birthday; 2.2 million random 7-character codes give a coin-flip collision.

definition: Extra data mixed into a hash input so identical inputs produce different outputs.
example: Hashing URL + user ID instead of the URL alone gives each user their own code.

definition: A mapping that pairs every input with exactly one output and every output with exactly one input, so nothing collides and it can be reversed.
example: Multiplying by a constant coprime to 62^7, modulo 62^7, is a bijection on 7-character codes.

definition: A rearrangement of a set's members; as a function, a bijection from a set onto itself.
example: Passing counter values through a permutation makes consecutive codes look unrelated.

definition: Two whole numbers are coprime when their only common factor is 1. Multiplying by a number coprime with m and taking the remainder mod m shuffles 0 to m − 1 without repeats.
example: Any odd number not divisible by 31 is coprime with 62^7, since 62 = 2 × 31.

definition: A structure for building reversible permutations (block ciphers) from repeated rounds of a keyed function. Designing a secure one is specialist work.
example: DES is built on a Feistel network.

definition: A long, unguessable token whose possession alone grants access to a resource, such as a secret sharing link.
example: A private link needs a long random token, not a 7-character code.

definition: A service that pre-generates random unique codes, stores them as unused and hands batches to servers that need them.
example: A key generation service avoids collision checks at creation time but must store billions of unused keys.

definition: A short code the user chooses instead of a generated one, such as sho.rt/summer-sale. It shares the namespace with generated codes, so uniqueness needs a conditional write.
example: Two users racing for "summer-sale" must not both win.

definition: A list of values that must be rejected or hidden, such as reserved words, abusive phrases or opted-out addresses.
example: A denylist stops anyone creating sho.rt/login or sho.rt/admin.

definition: Tricking people into giving up passwords or money with fake messages or sites. Short links are attractive to phishers because they hide the destination.
example: Scan new short links against a threat-intelligence service to catch phishing.

definition: Google's service listing unsafe web addresses (phishing, malware). Its free API is for non-commercial use; commercial users are directed to the Web Risk API.
example: Check each long URL against a threat list before creating a link.

definition: Online analytical processing: databases built for aggregate queries over huge amounts of data, such as ClickHouse or Druid, rather than for single-record lookups.
example: "Clicks by country, last 7 days" runs quickly on an OLAP store.

definition: An open-source real-time analytics database for fast aggregations over event data.
example: Druid can answer clicks-by-referrer queries interactively.

definition: The page a visitor came from, sent by browsers in the Referer header (spelt that way in HTTP).
example: Click counts by referrer show whether traffic came from email or social media.

definition: Sending a normal page whose script then changes window.location. It needs a full page load and fails for clients that do not run JavaScript.
example: curl -L follows a 302 but cannot follow a JavaScript redirect.

definition: The generic cell rate algorithm, from ATM networking: a rate limiter equivalent to a leaky bucket used as a meter, which stores just one timestamp per key (the theoretical arrival time of the next allowed request).
example: GCRA rejects a request that arrives before its theoretical arrival time minus the allowed burst.

definition: A short spike of requests well above the average rate.
example: A mobile app firing 15 requests at launch and then going quiet sends a burst.

definition: Redis's "set if not exists": it stores a key only if it does not exist yet, a simple way to claim something once.
example: SET idem:order-8812 1 NX succeeds for the first request only.

definition: Network address translation run by an internet provider, putting many customers (often thousands of mobile users) behind one public IPv4 address.
example: A tight per-IP limit can block every user behind one carrier-grade NAT address.

definition: Guessing a secret, such as a password or code, by trying many possibilities. Rate limits on login make it impractical.
example: Login limits should fail closed to keep brute-force protection during an outage.

definition: A challenge, such as picking images, meant to be easy for humans and hard for bots, used to slow automated abuse.
example: Require a CAPTCHA once a per-IP signup limit trips.

definition: Layering several independent protections so one failing does not leave the system exposed.
example: Per-IP limits, device tokens and a CAPTCHA together are defence in depth.

definition: In system design, short for a rate limiter (or a concurrency limiter): the component that decides whether each request is allowed or rejected according to per-key limits.
example: The limiter checks a token bucket in Redis and returns HTTP 429 when the bucket is empty.

definition: A limit on how many requests from one client can be in progress at once, as opposed to how many may start per second.
example: At most 5 in-flight report requests per customer.

definition: A grant that holds only for a limited time, such as a batch of tokens a gateway may spend or a right to own a conversation. Because it expires, a crashed holder cannot block others forever.
example: A gateway leases 10 tokens from Redis and spends them locally.

definition: A quick, pre-built way to turn a feature or rule off in production without a redeploy.
example: A wrong rate-limit rule that rejects everything should be undone with a kill switch.

definition: The k highest-ranked items from a set, for example the 10 most popular completions of a prefix.
example: Storing the top-10 list at every trie node makes a lookup one read.

definition: The beginning part of a string: "how t" is a prefix of "how to tie a tie".
example: Every query starting with "s" lives under the trie node for the prefix "s".

definition: A trie in which chains of single-child nodes are merged into one edge labelled with a string, saving memory on long unique tails.
example: A radix tree stores "pancakes" and "pancetta" as a shared "panc" edge then two short edges.

definition: An automaton that accepts every string within a given edit distance of a target, used for typo-tolerant matching. Edit (Levenshtein) distance is the smallest number of single-character insertions, deletions or substitutions that turns one string into another.
example: "pancaks" is one edit from "pancakes".

definition: Reducing the weight of older events by a constant factor per unit of time, so recent activity counts more. The half-life is the time for a weight to halve.
example: With 0.9 per day, a search's weight halves about every 6.6 days.

definition: A rule that only shows an item (such as a suggestion) once enough distinct users have produced it. It reduces exposure of rare personal queries but is not a privacy guarantee on its own.
example: Only suggest queries searched by at least 50 distinct users.

definition: Personally identifiable information: data that identifies a person, such as a name, home address or phone number.
example: Run PII detectors so addresses never become suggestions.

definition: An identifier that replaces a real identity (such as an account name) but still links one person's records together, so it is not anonymous.
example: Search logs keep a pseudonymous user ID so distinct users can be counted.

definition: A complete, immutable copy of a data structure at one point in time, built offline and loaded by servers as a unit.
example: Serving nodes load trie snapshot v42 next to v41, then swap.

definition: A language and region setting, such as en-GB, that decides language, formats and which suggestions apply.
example: Suggestions are cached per prefix and locale.

definition: Tailoring results to an individual user, for example from their history or location. It reduces how much can be cached for everyone.
example: Blend the user's recent searches into the global suggestion list on the client.

definition: The first stage of a ranking pipeline: cheaply gather a manageable set of possible items (candidates) for a slower model to rank.
example: The trie returns the top 50 suggestions as candidates for re-ranking.

definition: Ranking in steps: a cheap model narrows many candidates to a few, then an expensive model ranks only those, cutting cost.
example: Score 1,500 candidates with a light model and only the top 300 with the heavy one.

definition: A small, fast-updating dataset (such as trending queries) merged into results from a slower batch-built index.
example: The real-time layer surfaces "earthquake in Tokyo" within minutes.

definition: Converting text so that visually identical strings have the same code points (for example a precomposed é versus e plus an accent). Unicode is the standard that gives every character a number.
example: Normalise prefixes before lookup so "café" typed two ways finds the same node.

definition: Publishing a new version of a data structure by changing a single reference in one indivisible step, so readers see either the old or the new version, never a mix.
example: After loading trie v42, the node switches its root pointer from v41 to v42.

definition: Automatically flagging data that deviates sharply from normal patterns.
example: 500,000 searches from 300 accounts is an anomaly worth flagging.

definition: The social network run by Meta Platforms, whose engineering blog describes systems such as its typeahead, News Feed ranking and TAO.
example: Facebook's typeahead preloaded friends into the browser when the search box was focused.

definition: Meta's photo- and video-sharing social app, a common system design interview prompt.
example: "Design Instagram" needs upload, follow and feed requirements pinned down first.

definition: A message sent from a server through the phone platform's service (APNs for Apple, FCM for Android) that appears on a device even when the app is closed.
example: "Your order has shipped" arrives as a push notification.

definition: Apple Push Notification service: the only route for delivering push notifications to iPhones and other Apple devices. Servers send requests over HTTP/2 with a device token.
example: APNs returns 410 when a device token is no longer active.

definition: Firebase Cloud Messaging: Google's service for sending push messages to Android, iOS and web apps, addressed by registration tokens.
example: FCM returns an UNREGISTERED error for a stale registration token.

definition: An identifier that APNs or FCM issues for one app install on one device; the server needs it to address a push. Tokens go stale when apps are uninstalled or reinstalled.
example: Deactivate a device token when APNs says it is no longer valid.

definition: A tag on push messages so a newer message can replace an older pending one with the same tag instead of piling up (APNs apns-collapse-id, FCM collapse_key).
example: Five "Sam liked your photo" pushes with one collapse key show as one.

definition: One unit of an SMS: up to 160 GSM-7 characters, or 70 characters in the 16-bit UCS-2 encoding. Longer texts are split into several segments (153 or 67 characters each) and billed per segment.
example: A 200-character English text is sent as two segments.

definition: The default 7-bit character set for SMS, covering basic Latin letters and some symbols; each character is a 7-bit septet.
example: 160 GSM-7 characters fit in 140 bytes, one SMS segment.

definition: A way of encoding Unicode text in 16-bit code units; some characters (such as many emoji) need two units. SMS falls back to a 16-bit encoding (UCS-2, in practice UTF-16) for characters outside GSM-7.
example: An SMS containing an emoji switches to the 16-bit encoding and holds 70 units per segment, with the emoji using two of them.

definition: A one-time passcode: a short code sent (often by SMS) that is valid once and briefly, used to log in or confirm an action. It must arrive within seconds.
example: A login OTP stuck behind a marketing campaign is useless after its 5-minute TTL.

definition: A notification shown inside the app itself (a bell icon or feed) rather than through the phone's push system.
example: Every like is still recorded in the in-app inbox even when pushes are capped.

definition: A stored message pattern with placeholders, rendered per channel and language with the event's parameters.
example: "Your order {orderId} has shipped" rendered with orderId 8812.

definition: Adapting text and formats to a user's language and region.
example: The order_shipped template exists in en-GB, fr-FR and more.

definition: A notification sent to a large group of users at once, typically for marketing, which creates huge bursts of traffic.
example: A campaign to 50 million users over an hour adds about 14,000 sends a second.

definition: A defined group of users targeted by a campaign, such as "UK users active in the last 30 days".
example: The scheduler expands a segment into messages page by page.

definition: A limit on how many notifications of a type one user may receive in a period.
example: No more than 3 marketing pushes per user per day.

definition: Times, in the user's own time zone, during which non-urgent notifications are held back.
example: A low-priority push due at 3 am is delayed to 8 am.

definition: A named time zone from the IANA time zone database, such as Europe/London, which records offsets and daylight-saving rules over time. IANA is the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority.
example: Schedule "9 am local" by Europe/London, not by a fixed UTC offset.

definition: Moving clocks forward in summer, so a place's offset from UTC changes during the year.
example: New York is UTC−5 in winter and UTC−4 in summer.

definition: The UK's Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, which set rules for electronic marketing such as email and texts, generally requiring consent.
example: Marketing texts to UK individuals generally need consent under PECR.

definition: The US Telephone Consumer Protection Act, which restricts automated marketing calls and texts without consent.
example: Marketing SMS to US numbers must respect TCPA consent rules.

definition: The US law setting rules for commercial email, including honouring opt-out requests within 10 business days.
example: A marketing digest sent after an unsubscribe can breach CAN-SPAM.

definition: An email mechanism, defined in RFC 8058, letting mail clients unsubscribe a user with a single action via the List-Unsubscribe headers. Gmail requires it from bulk senders of marketing mail.
example: Gmail's bulk sender rules apply above 5,000 messages a day to personal accounts.

definition: The circuit-breaker state that lets a little test traffic through to a failed dependency; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it.
example: Send 1% of SMS to the primary provider as a probe while half-open.

definition: A notification from a provider (often via webhook) reporting what happened to a message: accepted, delivered, failed, bounced.
example: Twilio status webhooks update each SMS row from sent to delivered.

definition: A message rejected by the receiving mail system. A hard bounce is permanent, for example the mailbox does not exist, so the address should not be retried.
example: Mark an address invalid after a hard bounce.

definition: How trustworthy mailbox and phone providers judge a sender to be, based on bounces, complaints and spam; poor reputation gets messages filtered.
example: Repeatedly texting invalid numbers hurts sender reputation.

definition: A tiny invisible image in an email whose download signals the email was opened; image blocking and proxy prefetching make it unreliable.
example: An open is recorded when the pixel URL is fetched.

definition: One message summarising many events over a period instead of one notification each.
example: "Sam and 4 others liked your photo" in one daily digest.

definition: Sending through a cheap channel first (push) and a costlier one (SMS) only if the first goes unread within a set time.
example: If the push is not opened in 5 minutes, send an SMS.

definition: An outside company or platform service that actually delivers messages, such as Twilio for SMS, SES for email or APNs for push.
example: Provider rate limits, not your own servers, usually cap notification throughput.

definition: A cloud communications company whose APIs send SMS, voice calls and email.
example: A Twilio status webhook reports when an SMS is delivered.

definition: Vonage and Sinch are cloud communications providers that, like Twilio, send SMS to phone numbers, so they can serve as failover SMS providers.
example: Route SMS to Vonage if Twilio's error rate spikes.

definition: Amazon Simple Email Service, a managed service for sending email at scale.
example: SES events report bounces and complaints.

definition: An email-delivery service (owned by Twilio) for transactional and marketing email.
example: Email can fail over between SES and SendGrid.

definition: Google's email service, whose sender guidelines require bulk senders to support one-click unsubscribe for marketing mail.
example: Gmail treats senders of over 5,000 messages a day to personal accounts as bulk senders.

definition: A model in which something is always in one of a fixed set of states and moves between them only by defined transitions.
example: A send attempt moves claimed → sent → delivered, or claimed → failed.

definition: A user's permission to be sent a category of messages. Opting out (unsubscribing) withdraws it and must be honoured promptly. In general, opt-in means something is off until a person chooses it; opt-out means it is on until they refuse it.
example: Check the latest opt-out state at send time, not when the request was accepted.

definition: A personalised, scrolling list of recent posts from accounts a user follows (and, when ranked, recommended ones).
example: X's home timeline and Facebook's News Feed are news feeds.

definition: All posts written by one account, newest first.
example: Celebrity user timelines are read so often that they stay in cache.

definition: The difficulty that accounts with millions of followers make fan-out on write slow and expensive. Usually solved by pulling their posts at read time instead.
example: A 50-million-follower account would tie up the fan-out fleet for 50 seconds per post.

definition: Pushing posts from ordinary accounts into followers' timelines while pulling posts from very large accounts at read time and merging the two.
example: Push for accounts under 1 million followers, pull for those above.

definition: Turning a list of IDs into full objects by fetching the data for each (post text, author, counts), usually with a batched cache read.
example: A 50-ID timeline page is hydrated with one multi-get from the post cache.

definition: A single request that fetches many keys from a cache or store at once, saving round trips.
example: Hydrating 50 posts takes one multi-get rather than 50 separate reads.

definition: Combining k already-sorted lists into one sorted list, typically with a heap.
example: Merging recent posts from 1,000 followed accounts by time is a 1,000-way merge.

definition: The network of who follows (or is friends with) whom, stored so both "who follows X?" and "whom does Y follow?" are fast.
example: Fan-out workers ask the social graph for an author's followers.

definition: Meta's geographically distributed store for its social graph, built on MySQL with a caching layer.
example: TAO answers association queries such as "friends of X".

definition: Twitter's distributed graph database for storing follow relationships. Twitter no longer maintains it and archived the code in 2021.
example: FlockDB stored who-follows-whom for Twitter's fan-out.

definition: Redis commands on list values: LPUSH adds to the head, LTRIM cuts the list to a range, LRANGE reads a range and LREM removes matching items.
example: LPUSH then LTRIM 0 799 keeps a timeline capped at 800 IDs.

definition: A 64-bit floating-point number. It represents integers exactly only up to 2^53, so larger 64-bit IDs lose precision.
example: Redis sorted-set scores are doubles, so do not store 64-bit Snowflake IDs as scores.

definition: An account whose posts only approved followers may see, so visibility must be checked whenever posts are shown.
example: If an author locks their account, hydration must stop showing their posts to others.

definition: Using machine-learning models to order items by predicted relevance, such as the chance a user will like or reply to a post.
example: A "For you" feed scores 1,500 candidates with ML ranking.

definition: A machine-learning model made of layers of weighted connections that learns patterns from examples.
example: A heavy neural network predicts the probability of a like, reply or repost.

definition: Running a trained model on new input to get a prediction, as opposed to training it.
example: Scoring 135 million candidates a second is a large inference load.

definition: An input value a model uses to make a prediction, such as post age or how often the user interacts with the author.
example: Author affinity and engagement so far are ranking features.

definition: How long a user spends looking at an item, used as a signal of interest.
example: A long dwell time on a post suggests the user found it interesting.

definition: In feeds, posts from accounts the user does not follow (out-of-network) versus from accounts they do follow (in-network).
example: A "For you" feed mixes in-network posts with recommended out-of-network ones.

definition: One showing of an item to a user, logged to measure engagement and train ranking models.
example: Impressions and likes feed back into model training.

definition: Ordering events so that anything that depends on another (such as a reply to a post) is never shown before it.
example: Show a reply only after the post it answers.

definition: The social network now called X, whose timeline architecture and Snowflake IDs are classic design references.
example: Twitter used fan-out on write with special handling for celebrity accounts.

definition: A fast store (often Redis with TTLs) mapping each connected device to the gateway holding its connection, so messages can be routed to it.
example: The registry says device bob-phone → gateway 87, connection 2.

definition: Taking a server out of service gently: stop sending it new work, let existing work finish or move clients off in batches, then shut it down.
example: Drain a gateway during a deploy instead of dropping 250,000 sockets at once.

definition: A programming language and runtime built for highly concurrent, fault-tolerant systems with millions of lightweight processes; WhatsApp's servers use it.
example: WhatsApp reported over 2 million connections on one Erlang server in 2012.

definition: A programming language that runs on Erlang's BEAM virtual machine; Discord uses it for its real-time layer.
example: Discord scaled Elixir to millions of concurrent users.

definition: The virtual machine that runs Erlang and Elixir code, designed for huge numbers of lightweight processes.
example: Each WebSocket can be handled by its own lightweight BEAM process.

definition: An open-source Unix-like operating system, used by WhatsApp for its early servers.
example: WhatsApp's 2012 two-million-connection test ran on FreeBSD.

definition: In chat, showing whether a user is online now or when they were last seen.
example: Push presence only to people who have a chat with that user open.

definition: The "is typing..." signal in a chat; ephemeral, never stored, and safe to drop under load.
example: Typing indicators go over the socket only.

definition: A message telling the sender that their message reached the recipient's device (delivered) or was opened (read), such as WhatsApp's grey and blue ticks.
example: Two blue ticks: the recipient opened the chat.

definition: A stored position meaning "everything up to this sequence number has been delivered (or read)", so one receipt covers many messages.
example: read upToSeq 950 acknowledges every message up to 950 at once.

definition: In chat, a server-side list of messages not yet acknowledged by a particular device; nothing is removed until the device acks.
example: An offline phone's inbox holds its messages until it reconnects.

definition: Encryption where only the communicating devices hold the keys, so servers relaying the messages cannot read them.
example: With E2EE, search and notification text must be handled on the device.

definition: An end-to-end encryption protocol for messaging, used by Signal and WhatsApp, with per-device keys and forward secrecy.
example: WhatsApp uses the Signal Protocol for 1:1 and group chats.

definition: A Signal Protocol scheme for groups: each sender shares a sender key with members once, then encrypts each group message a single time.
example: With sender keys a 1,000-device group message is encrypted once, not 1,000 times.

definition: Encrypted data, unreadable without the key (the readable original is called plaintext).
example: The chat server stores and routes ciphertext it cannot read.

definition: Letting one account use several devices at once (phone, desktop, web), each with its own connection, inbox, cursors and, with E2EE, its own keys.
example: A message to someone with a phone and two laptops is encrypted for three devices.

definition: A fixed time window used as part of a partition key, so a busy entity's data is split across many bounded partitions.
example: Partition messages by (channel_id, bucket) so no partition grows forever.

definition: A systems programming language with memory safety and no garbage collector; Discord wrote its data services in it.
example: Discord's Rust data services coalesce requests in front of ScyllaDB.

definition: A compiled systems programming language; ScyllaDB is written in it.
example: ScyllaDB reimplements Cassandra in C++.

definition: Meta's end-to-end encrypted messaging app, built on Erlang servers.
example: WhatsApp's multi-device design encrypts per device.

definition: A chat platform for communities with very large channels; its engineering blog describes its message storage and Elixir real-time layer.
example: Discord stores trillions of messages.

definition: A workplace messaging platform whose server keeps channel history.
example: Slack's real-time messaging uses gateways and channel servers.

definition: Telegram and Meta's Messenger are messaging apps; both keep message history on their servers.
example: Telegram channels can have very large audiences.

definition: An index that answers location queries such as "everything within 2 km of this point" quickly.
example: Driver locations go in an in-memory geo index.

definition: An extension that adds geospatial types, functions and indexes to PostgreSQL.
example: PostGIS can find drivers within 2 km of a point.

definition: A way of encoding a latitude and longitude as a short string, where nearby places usually share a prefix.
example: Redis geo commands use geohash-based sorted sets.

definition: The code that sits between business logic and the database, so storage can change (for example to shards) without rewriting callers.
example: Hide sharding by user ID behind the data-access layer.

definition: The code run on every request, where added latency or cost matters most.
example: Keep analytics writes off the redirect hot path.

definition: A private message between users of a social app, outside the public feed.
example: "I'll skip DMs and stories unless you want them."

definition: The standard reply keyword that opts a phone number out of further SMS from a sender; it must be honoured as withdrawn consent.
example: A user who replies STOP must not receive more marketing texts.

definition: Adapting software text and formats to a user's language and region, for example rendering a notification template in en-GB or fr-FR.
example: The order_shipped template has a version per channel and per locale.

definition: In a user interface, waiting until typing pauses (say 100 ms) before sending a request, so a burst of keystrokes becomes one request.
example: A fast typist's 8 keystrokes in 800 ms may produce only a few suggestion requests.

definition: Bitly and TinyURL are popular URL-shortening services.
example: A TinyURL/Bitly-style service maps short codes to long URLs.

definition: A US ride-hailing company; its engineers created the Envoy proxy and its rate limit service.
example: Lyft open-sourced the Envoy rate limit service.

definition: Sending every request for the same key (a conversation, a channel) to the same server instance, usually with consistent hashing, so that instance can order, cache or coalesce work for it.
example: Route all requests for channel 42 to one data-service instance so identical reads can be coalesced.

definition: Short for key-value, as in a key-value store: a database that stores and fetches values by a unique key.
example: A flattened prefix → list KV store is easy to shard.

definition: The sequence of components a write request passes through, from the client to durable storage and any follow-on work such as fan-out.
example: Post service → posts store + outbox → Kafka → fan-out workers → Redis timelines.

definition: The sequence of components a read request passes through before the response is returned; it is usually the latency-critical path.
example: Timeline service → Redis list of IDs → hydration from the post cache.

definition: The online part of a system that answers user requests, kept as simple and fast as possible; heavy computation happens elsewhere.
example: Typeahead's serving path is an in-memory trie lookup cached at the edge.

definition: The offline part of a system that collects, aggregates and builds data (such as a new trie snapshot) for the serving path to load.
example: Search logs → counts → ranked lists → a new trie snapshot every day.

definition: Rate limiting in two layers: each gateway enforces approximately from local state (such as leased tokens) and periodically syncs with a central store.
example: Gateways sync their local counts with Redis every ~100 ms.

definition: Short for authentication (proving who a caller is) and often authorisation (what they may do).
example: Auth on both endpoints, for example OAuth bearer tokens.

definition: In a notification platform, the worker that calls one delivery channel's provider (push, SMS, email), records the result and handles retries.
example: The SMS channel sender opens a circuit breaker when Twilio's error rate spikes.

definition: In a chat design, the backend service that owns a conversation: it deduplicates, assigns sequence numbers, persists messages and routes them to recipients' gateways.
example: The chat service owning conversation 42 assigns seq 901.

definition: The component that sends push notifications through APNs or FCM to wake offline devices.
example: If Bob is offline, the push service asks APNs to wake his phone.

definition: The symbol meaning "approximately equal to": the value has been rounded or rests on an assumption.
example: 86,400 ≈ 100,000 for mental maths.

definition: The symbol meaning "much greater than", usually a factor of ten or more.
example: 2,000 leased tokens ≫ a 100-token limit.

definition: The Greek capital letter sigma, meaning "add up all of these".
example: Σ count_d over the last 30 days adds 30 daily counts.

definition: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original: √9 = 3. In the birthday problem, the number of random ids you can issue before a collision becomes likely grows with the square root of the number of possible ids.
The inverse of raising to a power: log_b(x) answers "b to what power gives x?". The natural logarithm ln uses the base e ≈ 2.718.
The Greek letter lambda, used in queueing (for example Little's law) for the average arrival rate of requests.
example: λ = 100 requests per minute ≈ 1.67 per second.

definition: In these lessons an arrow means "maps to", "becomes" or "leads to", for example code → long URL.
example: 125 → "21" means 125 is written as "21" in base62.

definition: The currency of the United States; cost estimates in these lessons are in dollars.
example: $0.01 per SMS × 36 million = $360,000 a day.
